rationale: A wins because it knows which angle not to pitch. It refuses "At-home lab testing as a standalone digital health trend angle" until the mechanism is proven, while B keeps "Telehealth GLP-1 plus at-home blood tests: the build of a personalized weight-loss stack" and tries to make a product feature wear a category-story hat. Both sets have useful regulatory and business angles, but A is tougher about proof before outreach.
gaps_in_A: "Novo Nordisk Spent Years Building the GLP-1 Market" names Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly even though the update only says branded manufacturers pushed back. Likely, but still not in the supplied facts.

"Hims & Hers Just Hit Profitability. Its First Big Move Carries FDA Risk" overclaims. The update says Hims recently turned profitable; it does not say this is the first major strategic move after that milestone.
"clearest test case yet" is a little grand. The update supports a test case, not necessarily the clearest one in the market.
gaps_in_B: "A newly profitable Hims & Hers bets its margins on compounded weight-loss drugs" invents a margin thesis. Profitability is supplied; margin dependence is not.

"Telehealth GLP-1 plus at-home blood tests: the build of a personalized weight-loss stack" is the softest kept angle. It admits it collapses without proof, which means it should probably have been refused until the lab mechanism is known.
"Decay: 4hr" on the FDA angle is fake precision. Nothing in the update supports a four-hour clock; it reads like urgency theater.

B misses the patient-access customer-story lens. The update's strongest human fact is "at a fraction of branded-drug prices," and B mostly hands that to competitor and markets reporters instead of asking who was priced out.
